narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 63.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you. Your family income bracket had the strongest influence, followed by your first-year grades in law school, and then your LSAT score. 

Your middle family income pushed the prediction toward failure. While many accepted students also come from middle-income families, this bracket overall tends to be associated with a slightly higher risk of struggling on the bar compared with students from higher-income backgrounds. Your first-year law school grades (decile 5) also worked against you; this is noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (decile 6), signaling that your early performance placed you behind most successful applicants. Surprisingly, your LSAT score of 39 actually pulled the prediction in a positive direction because it sits above the average of 37.2 among accepted students. However, this helpful effect was not strong enough to overcome the other two factors.

Your third-year grades and undergraduate GPA were solid and worked in your favor, but they carried less weight in the final decision.

You should focus on strengthening your first-year academic performance and consider additional bar exam preparation resources. Retaking the LSAT or gaining more targeted experience could also help improve your profile for future applications.
